data.title: CCPA Imposes Rs 1 Lakh Penalty On Britannia Over 100% Whole Wheat Bread’ Claim
data.description:
The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) has imposed a penalty of Rs 1 lakh on Britannia Industries Ltd. for misleading advertisements and unfair trade practices concerning its ‘100% Whole Wheat Bread’ product. The authority has directed the company to discontinue the advertisements with immediate effect and submit a compliance report within 15 days.

In an order dated October 22, 2026, the CCPA held that the prominent ‘100% Whole Wheat Bread’ claim was misleading because the product contained only 62% whole wheat flour, while the remaining 38% comprised other ingredients, including water, yeast, wheat bran and other constituents.

The authority concluded that the claim conveyed the impression that the product consisted entirely of whole wheat flour, contrary to its actual composition. It also held that the accompanying ‘0% Maida’ claim did not cure or mitigate the misleading impression.

CCPA Rejects Britannia’s Defence

The proceedings arose from suo motu cognizance taken by the CCPA over Britannia’s product packaging and advertisements across its website and social media platforms.

Following a preliminary inquiry, the authority issued a notice to the company on January 13, 2025. Britannia submitted its response on January 28, 2025, arguing that the claim referred to the composition of the flour used in the product rather than the composition of the finished bread.

The company maintained that the product contained 62% whole wheat flour and that the remaining ingredients were necessary for manufacturing bread. It also contended that the expression ‘100% Whole Wheat Flour’ was calculated on a flour basis and that the claim was intended to communicate the absence of refined flour or maida.

The CCPA subsequently examined an investigation report dated September 7, 2026, received from the Director General (Investigation), along with findings and observations furnished by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI).

According to the order, the FSSAI observed that the use of ‘100%’ in isolation or in conjunction with descriptors could create a false impression of absolute purity or superiority. The investigation also found that the product’s whole wheat flour content was below the prescribed threshold for using the nomenclature ‘Whole Wheat Bread’.

FSSAI Standards And The 75% Threshold

The CCPA referred to Regulation 2.6 of the Food Safety and Standards (Labelling and Display) Second Amendment Regulations, 2022, which stipulates that whole wheat flour must constitute at least 75% of the prescribed composition for a product to be displayed as ‘Whole Wheat Bread’.

The authority noted that Britannia’s product contained 62% whole wheat flour, below the prescribed threshold. It rejected the company’s argument that the claim should be assessed exclusively on a flour basis, holding that the overall composition and presentation of the finished product were relevant to determining whether consumers were misled.

The order further recorded that the FSSAI had issued an advisory dated May 28, 2025, advising food business operators to discontinue the use of the term ‘100%’ on food product labels, packaging and promotional materials.

The CCPA also noted that, according to the investigation findings, Britannia continued displaying the claim on its website and promotional channels despite the advisory and subsequent regulatory communications.

CCPA Finds Disclaimer Insufficient

The authority observed that the product’s front packaging prominently displayed ‘100% Whole Wheat Bread’, alongside the ‘0% Maida’ claim. A qualifying statement on the reverse side read: ‘Made from 100% Whole Wheat Flour on Flour Basis’.

The CCPA held that the disclaimer, linked to the front-label claim through a symbol and presented in comparatively small print, did not adequately correct the impression created by the prominent claim.

It observed that an ordinary consumer might not examine the detailed ingredient declaration before purchasing the product. The authority also found that the placement and presentation of the qualification made it insufficiently prominent to clarify the actual composition.

The CCPA further considered the accompanying representation that the bread ‘pairs perfectly well with a healthy diet’, holding that the overall packaging could create an impression about the product’s dietary suitability that was not adequately substantiated by its composition.

Findings Under The Consumer Protection Act, 2019

The CCPA held that the representations violated Section 2(28) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, which defines misleading advertisements, and constituted an unfair trade practice under Section 2(47).

The authority also referred to Section 2(9), concerning consumer rights, including the right to be informed about the quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard and price of goods.

In addition, the order referred to Regulation 4(1) of the Food Safety and Standards (Advertising and Claims) Regulations, 2018, and the Guidelines for Prevention of Misleading Advertisements and Endorsements for Misleading Advertisements, 2022.

The CCPA concluded that the prominent numerical claim, combined with the limited prominence of the qualifying disclosure, misrepresented the product’s composition and could influence consumers’ purchasing decisions.

Exercising its powers under Sections 10, 18, 20 and 21 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, the CCPA issued the following directions to Britannia Industries Ltd.:

1. Discontinuation of advertisements: Immediately discontinue the false and misleading advertisements across print and electronic media, including social media.

2. Monetary penalty: Pay a penalty of Rs 1,00,000 for engaging in misleading advertisements and unfair trade practices.

3. Compliance report: Submit a report to the CCPA on compliance with the directions within 15 days from the date of the order.

The order reinforces the CCPA’s position that food-product claims must be assessed in the context of the product’s actual composition and the overall impression conveyed to an ordinary consumer. It also underscores that a qualifying statement in fine print may not be sufficient to neutralise a prominent, potentially misleading claim on product packaging.

data.title: Coal Gasification Can Cut Import Dependence, But Costs Remain A Hurdle
data.description:
Jindal Steel highlights up to 90 per cent domestic sourcing for new gasification equipment, while industry experts flag high-ash Indian coal, project economics and carbon management as key considerations for commercial deployment

India’s coal gasification ambitions will depend on lowering capital costs, strengthening domestic equipment manufacturing and integrating carbon management solutions, industry executives said at Gasification India 2026 in New Delhi, as the country seeks to reduce dependence on imported industrial inputs and make greater use of domestic coal resources.

Speaking at the 17th edition of the conference, held on 22-23 October, Naveen Ahlawat, Head – Green Hydrogen, Green Steel, Gasification Projects and CCSU at Jindal Steel Limited, said the company’s experience with coal gasification highlighted the importance of supply-chain localisation and technology optimisation in making projects commercially viable.

Ahlawat said Jindal Steel had reduced its dependence on imported equipment and components for its ongoing gasification expansion, with domestic sourcing now accounting for around 90 per cent  of requirements, compared with approximately 55 per cent when the earlier plant was developed. “Cost is super important. The project cost, and everybody is aware that the growth of this project is capital expenditure-heavy. Optimisation, localisation of the supply chain, and reducing the cost are super important,” he said.

Domestic Manufacturing

Ahlawat said the company was applying lessons from its existing coal gasification operations to a new phase of development, including manufacturing gasifiers and associated equipment within India. The initiative also involves using steel plates produced at its own steel plant and working with domestic suppliers to reduce dependence on imported components. He said the company was also evaluating changes to gas purification technology to bring down investment requirements.

According to Ahlawat, replacing the Rectisol process with pressure swing adsorption (PSA) for syngas-based direct reduced iron production could substantially reduce costs where the more complex purification process is unnecessary. The localisation push comes as India explores coal gasification for producing synthesis gas, or syngas, a mixture primarily comprising hydrogen and carbon monoxide. Syngas can serve as an industrial feedstock and reducing agent in steelmaking, while also supporting the production of chemicals and other industrial products.

Ahlawat said coal gasification could help reduce exposure to imported industrial inputs, but stressed that project developers must assess coal characteristics, technology maturity, conversion efficiency and the value of by-products before committing capital. He also pointed to opportunities to use syngas in existing industrial processes, including blast furnaces and galvanising and colour-coating lines, potentially reducing the consumption of other fuels.

Carbon Management Challenge

However, the commercial case for coal gasification cannot be separated from its emissions profile, particularly as steelmakers face increasing pressure to decarbonise production. Ahlawat said gasification should be viewed as a transitional step rather than a substitute for the eventual shift towards green hydrogen and lower-carbon industrial processes. He cautioned that without integration with renewable energy and carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS), coal gasification’s carbon intensity could remain comparable to conventional coal-based processes.

“Gasification has to be looked at as a bridge fuel or as a bridge step,” he said, adding that the longer-term direction for the steel sector remained lower-carbon production.

Hidayatullah Mohammad, Senior Engineer – Gasification Technology at Air Products, said the quality of Indian coal presented a significant technical and economic challenge because of its high ash content and the resulting demands on gasification systems. An internal assessment by Air Products, cited by Mohammad, found that increasing coal ash content from 16 per cent to 32 per cent raised coal consumption by around 34-35 per cent and oxygen consumption by approximately 20 per cent to produce the same quantity of syngas. Mohammad said technology selection and reactor design therefore needed to account for local coal characteristics, ash behaviour and the economics of operating the plant.

“It will never be a technology limitation to handle any challenging coal. We just have to see what is the right economic model that can fit in, and we have to choose the right design basis for that,” he said. Vartika Shukla, former Chairman and Managing Director of Engineers India Limited, chaired the session on advancing coal gasification technologies for commercial deployment. The discussions highlighted the central challenge facing India’s gasification strategy: translating domestic resource availability into commercially competitive industrial production while limiting emissions and reducing dependence on imported technology and equipment.

Sonali Chawhan

BW Reporters The author is a Trainee Correspondent at BW Businessworld.

data.title: India’s Coal Gasification Push Faces Financing And Cost Hurdles, Industry Leaders Say
data.description:
India’s target of gasifying 100 million tonnes of coal annually will depend on project execution, reliable feedstock supplies and long-term purchase agreements, industry leaders said at Gasification India 2026

India’s coal gasification ambitions will require stronger financing mechanisms, assured demand and coordinated project execution to translate policy support into commercially viable investments, industry leaders said at the 17th edition of Gasification India 2026 in New Delhi on 22 October.

The two-day conference, being held on 22–23 October, brought together policymakers, coal producers, project developers, technology providers and investors to discuss the commercial deployment of coal and lignite gasification. The discussions come as India seeks to reduce import dependence, strengthen domestic manufacturing and expand the industrial use of indigenous coal resources.

Ashwinkumar Khatri, Director General of Mission Energy Foundation and organiser of the conference, said the priority was to move beyond policy commitments and address the financial, technological and operational barriers facing projects. He said financing, feedstock quality and offtake arrangements would be critical to building a competitive domestic coal gasification ecosystem.

Financing And Offtake Remain Key Hurdles

Amrit Lal Meena, Chairman of the Gasification Technologies & Research Council of India and former Secretary of the Ministry of Coal, identified four priorities for improving investor confidence: long-term financing, assured offtake, reliable feedstock supplies and faster project implementation. He said government support through capital incentives and coal availability had created opportunities for the sector, but projects would need predictable financial and commercial arrangements to become viable. Meena called for measures such as credit guarantees, repayment moratoria and timely disbursement of incentives. Recognising eligible coal gasification projects as infrastructure under the National Infrastructure Pipeline could also improve access to affordable financing, he said.

Long-term purchase agreements with the fertiliser, gas, chemicals and steel industries would help developers secure demand. Transparent offtake guarantees and price-stabilisation mechanisms could provide additional support to early projects. He also stressed the need for enforceable coal supply agreements covering quantity, quality, pricing and delivery, alongside adequate water, power and transport infrastructure.

Meena said the first group of integrated projects required coordinated assistance for land acquisition, statutory clearances and financial support. India aims to gasify 100 million tonnes of coal annually, with timely execution and investor confidence emerging as important factors in meeting the target.

Coal India Projects Move Ahead

Peeyush Kumar, Managing Director of BCGCL, the Coal India–Bharat Heavy Electricals joint venture, said construction had begun on three coal gasification projects being undertaken by Coal India and its partners. The projects involve collaborations with Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd (BHEL), GAIL India and Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd (BPCL). Kumar said controlling project costs, strengthening engineering, procurement and construction capabilities, and improving project management would be essential to implementation. He also highlighted the potential of coal gasification to support import substitution, particularly in urea production.

However, reducing the ash content of Indian coal through washing would need greater policy attention to contain costs and improve the economics of initial projects. Kumar called for wider investor participation, exploration of new products and stronger cooperation among stakeholders. Separately, Alvarez & Marsal unveiled its report, Coal Gasification for ‘Atmanirbhar Bharat’ – Shaping the Next Industrial Revolution, at the conference. The event’s organisers said a policy paper would be prepared based on the conference discussions, with recommendations to be taken up with the government. The proposals are expected to focus on addressing implementation barriers and accelerating the development of India’s coal gasification sector.

Sonali Chawhan

BW Reporters The author is a Trainee Correspondent at BW Businessworld.

data.title: Nomura Favours ACME Solar As Storage Gains Importance In India’s Clean Energy Market
data.description:
The brokerage assigns a Buy rating to ACME Solar and a Neutral rating to NTPC Green Energy, citing storage opportunities, project execution and transmission constraints

Nomura has picked ACME Solar Holdings as its preferred renewable energy play over NTPC Green Energy, betting on the growing value of battery storage and round-the-clock power supply as India scales up clean energy capacity.

The Japanese brokerage initiated coverage with a Buy rating and a target price of Rs 505 for ACME Solar, while assigning NTPC Green Energy a Neutral rating and a target price of Rs 100. The contrasting assessments highlight a growing divide in India’s clean energy market: developers are increasingly being evaluated not only on planned renewable capacity but also on their ability to commission projects, integrate storage and deliver electricity when demand peaks.

India’s renewable energy capacity has expanded rapidly, but intermittent solar and wind generation has created challenges for grid management. Surplus solar power during the day and higher electricity demand outside solar hours have strengthened the case for battery energy storage systems (BESS) and firm, dispatchable renewable energy projects. According to market reports, the share of grid-storage-backed tenders rose from 22 per cent in financial year 2021–22 to 87 per cent in 2025–26, underlining the increasing importance of storage in renewable energy procurement.

Storage Strengthens ACME Solar’s Growth Outlook

Nomura expects ACME Solar’s revenue to grow at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 66 per cent and earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) at 65 per cent between FY27 and FY29. The brokerage expects the company to add 4.3 gigawatts (GW) of contracted capacity during the period. The company is transitioning from a conventional solar independent power producer to a platform offering firm and dispatchable renewable power. More than half of its portfolio capacity is linked to firm and dispatchable renewable energy projects, which combine generation with storage to meet specified electricity supply schedules.

ACME Solar’s total portfolio stood at around 8.4 GW, including a recently awarded 300 MW project. Of this, approximately 3 GW was operational, while projects under execution provided further growth potential. Falling battery costs and early commissioning of storage assets could also improve project economics. Bringing storage online ahead of scheduled project completion can allow developers to monetise electricity through merchant and short-term markets, while improving returns on invested equity.

Transmission Constraints Cloud NTPC Green’s Prospects

Nomura expects NTPC Green Energy’s revenue and EBITDA to grow at CAGRs of 74 per cent and 72 per cent, respectively, between FY27 and FY29. The projections are supported by planned capacity additions, an extensive project pipeline and the parent company NTPC’s execution experience and relatively low borrowing costs. NTPC Green has approximately 12.9 GW of capacity under construction through its wholly owned subsidiary and another 3.4 GW under joint ventures. The company is targeting 60 GW of renewable energy capacity by FY32. However, Nomura has flagged transmission availability as a key risk, warning that connectivity constraints could delay project commissioning and limit capacity additions compared with the company’s guidance.

The broader investment trend suggests that India’s renewable energy expansion is entering a more execution-sensitive phase. As storage becomes integral to power procurement, access to transmission infrastructure, battery costs and commissioning schedules are likely to influence developers’ earnings visibility and capital efficiency. For investors, the distinction between announced capacity and operational assets remains critical, particularly as renewable developers compete to deliver dependable electricity rather than generation capacity alone.

data.title: Uno Minda Targets Rs 40,000 Cr Revenue By FY30 On EV Push
data.description:
The auto component maker plans to expand its electric vehicle powertrain, seating, sunroof and advanced electronics businesses as it looks to capitalise on vehicle electrification and rising demand for premium features

Uno Minda is targeting nearly double its revenue to Rs 40,000 crore by financial year 2030, banking on electric vehicle (EV) powertrains, complete seating systems, sunroofs and advanced electronics to drive its next phase of growth. The auto component manufacturer plans to expand its product portfolio and manufacturing capabilities as automakers increase investments in electrification, technology and premium vehicle features. The company’s revenue stood at around Rs 19,700 crore in FY26, according to media reports. Its growth strategy reflects a broader shift in India’s automotive component industry, where suppliers are seeking to increase the value of components supplied per vehicle rather than relying solely on growth in vehicle production volumes.

EV Investments Drive Expansion

Uno Minda is expanding its presence in electric-drive systems and other technology-intensive automotive components as manufacturers adapt to changing powertrain requirements. Its plans also cover seating systems, sunroofs and electronic features, which are gaining importance as passenger vehicles become more technologically advanced. The company’s expansion comes amid growing demand for EV-related components and increasing localisation of automotive technologies in India. It has also pursued technology partnerships and capacity additions to strengthen its position across conventional and electric vehicle platforms.

For FY27, Uno Minda has outlined capital expenditure of approximately Rs 1,750 crore, covering growth projects and investments required to maintain existing operations. Several manufacturing projects are expected to begin production or ramp up during the year, according to company updates. The strategy is aimed at diversifying revenue streams while strengthening its relationships with original equipment manufacturers (OEMs). Higher component value per vehicle, product innovation and export opportunities could support growth beyond overall vehicle sales.

Premium Features Lift Prospects

The expansion also reflects the growing importance of premiumisation in India's passenger vehicle market. Features such as advanced lighting, infotainment systems, sunroofs and integrated seating solutions are becoming important areas of competition among automakers, creating opportunities for component suppliers. Industry analysts note that suppliers able to combine technology development, local manufacturing and product diversification may benefit from this shift. However, the pace of growth will depend on new plant utilisation, customer demand, project execution and the ability to manage rising input and labour costs.

The EV transition also presents a longer-term opportunity for component makers to move into higher-value products, including electric-drive units, controllers and related electronic systems. At the same time, capital-intensive expansion can put pressure on margins before new facilities reach optimal utilisation. For Uno Minda, achieving its FY30 revenue ambition will therefore depend not only on India's vehicle market expansion but also on converting investments and order wins into sustained sales. Its ability to scale newer businesses while maintaining profitability will remain a key factor in determining whether its technology-led growth strategy delivers the targeted results.

data.title: “We Will Focus On Increasing Make In India Lines For Women”: Casio MD
data.description:
Takuto Kimura says the company plans to introduce new locally manufactured watch models in 2027 as it seeks to double women’s watch sales by expanding its product portfolio

Casio India sees scope to double women’s watch sales by expanding its locally manufactured portfolio, developing new models across watch categories and capitalising on demand for fashion-led timepieces. The Japanese watchmaker is also looking to strengthen its brand presence and widen its retail reach, including in smaller cities and banking on demand for traditional watches among younger consumers.

“We will especially try to focus on increasing the Make in India line-ups and focus on the women's line-up…if we strengthen our strategy and product line-up in the women market, I'm confident that we can increase the sales double,” Takuto Kimura, Managing Director, Casio India, said in an interview with BW Businessworld on the sidelines of the Launch of G-Shock 2500 series.

The company has not disclosed the current contribution of women's watches to its Indian sales, a timeline for doubling the segment's sales or a quantified investment plan. Kimura said strengthening the product range and market strategy would be central to pursuing the opportunity, with additional India-made models potentially arriving in 2027.

Casio introduced a range of 28 locally manufactured watch models in January 2026, including 23 designs aimed at women, according to previously reported company announcements. The next phase of product development could include additions under G-Shock and Edifice, and other segments also, although the company has not confirmed launch dates or the number of models planned.

Casio reported double-digit sales growth for both G-Shock and its Casio Watch brand. Its results briefing said Casio Watch attracted new users, including women and younger consumers, and identified marketing to women as part of its strategy. The company also said demand for smartwatches appeared to have passed its peak.

Additionally, Casio India's revenue more than doubled to Rs 894 crore in FY25 from Rs 394 crore in FY21, while net profit rose to Rs 53.6 crore from Rs 8.3 crore over the same period, according to regulatory filings accessed through business intelligence platform Tofler.

Traditional Watches Remain Priority

Casio India is not currently planning to enter the smartwatch segment, despite the category's earlier rapid expansion. Kimura said the company would continue to focus on traditional watches, keeping its domestic strategy centred on established product categories rather than adding smartwatch offerings.

“As of now we focus on traditional watch,” Kimura said.

India's smartwatch market has contracted for two consecutive years, according to International Data Corporation (IDC). Shipments fell 17.6 per cent to 28.9 million units in 2025. In April-June 2026, shipments declined 4 per cent to 6.38 million units, marking the tenth consecutive quarter of contraction, although the decline was narrower than the 28.4 per cent fall recorded a year earlier.

The slowdown has not been uniform across the wider watch industry. Titan Company reported 23 per cent growth in its watches division in the June quarter of FY27, according to its business update. Analogue watches grew in the high twenties, while its smartwatch business declined in the low teens, highlighting the contrasting performance of traditional and connected timepieces.

“The young generation in India more tends to have a watch. Not only just timekeeping but also they try to wear it to express their own style and fashion,” he said.

He identified G-Shock as a brand that resonates with younger consumers who follow global trends in fashion, art, music and sport through social media. Casio Vintage, meanwhile, has benefited from interest in 1990s fashion, he said.

In India, Casio attributed continued G-Shock growth partly to the impact of two major brand ambassadors. Sales of Casio Watch also remained strong as its distributor network expanded beyond major cities into smaller urban markets. India and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations together accounted for 16 per cent of Casio's timepiece sales in the quarter; the company did not provide a separate India figure.

Casio India's immediate priorities remain watches, calculators and electronic musical instruments. Kimura said the company had no current plans to launch its earU hearing-assistance earbuds in India.

Retail Expansion Across India

Alongside product development, Casio India plans to increase its physical retail presence and strengthen online sales. The company had 85 brand stores at the time of the interview, Kimura said, as it seeks to build its reach across major cities and smaller markets. The company has a target to open 200 stores by 2030 and, with the ambition to double its India business over five years, Shin Takano, the company’s global CEO, has said previously.

“One of the key strategies we have to focus on is how to increase the number of brand stores nationwide in India…So from tier 1, we try to open a new flagship brand store. And tier 2, we expand the number of brand stores,” Kimura said, adding that while continuing to consider opportunities in tier 3 cities. At the same time, online sales would remain another area of focus.

Kimura said online and offline sales of watches were broadly comparable, although he did not provide a detailed channel-wise breakdown or distinguish between sales through Casio's own website and third-party ecommerce platforms.

In a September 2025, Kimura said Casio held a 12 per cent share of India's watch market, ranking second, compared with 8 per cent in 2014. He also outlined an ambition to triple sales by 2035. These figures were company-reported claims and were not independently established in the latest interview.

Competition In Women's Watches

Men's watches account for an estimated 57.68 per cent of India's watch market, while women's watches are the fastest-growing segment, with estimated growth of 9.16 per cent, according to Mordor Intelligence. The figures point to an opportunity for brands to broaden their appeal among women, although the estimates depend on the research firm's market definitions and forecast period.

Casio India is looking to strengthen its presence in the segment through product development and local manufacturing. Its women's portfolio will span categories including G-Shock and Edifice, Kimura said, as the company seeks to address a gap in its existing range.

“I think the women's category, of course some other brands have more line-up than Casio. However, as I said, the women market now has a big potential, so we strengthen this market,” he said.

Casio faces competition from established watchmakers and brands with dedicated women's collections. Titan's Raga range, alongside offerings from Fossil and Citizen, gives consumers alternatives designed around women's styling preferences. Casio's challenge is to expand its range and strengthen its relevance in a segment where competitors already have established product offerings.

Kimura said Indian consumers consider both price and brand value when choosing watches, although the importance of price varies across market segments. Casio's strategy is to build brand recognition through marketing while pricing products to suit their intended consumers. He did not provide a breakdown of sales or profitability for women's watches.

Priyanshu Priya

BW Reporters The author is trainee correspondent at BW Businessworld.

data.title: Google’s Pichai says AI self-improvement still in early stages
data.description:
Google CEO Sundar Pichai has indicated that the development of AI recursive self-improvement (RSI) remains in an early stage, suggesting that current AI systems are not yet fully autonomous in their model-building capabilities. This statement comes amid ongoing efforts by Google's DeepMind division, which utilizes AI loops and agents to assist human researchers in developing AI models. Despite advancements, Google has not observed notable end-to-end acceleration in AI research and development across various benchmarks. Pichai's remarks suggest that the industry is still far from achieving fully autonomous AI systems capable of self-improvement without human intervention.

  • Sundar Pichai's statement suggests that the development of AI RSI is still in its early stages.
  • The current market pricing for Anthropic's AI model reflects decreased confidence in its chances of being the best by October 2026.
  • Google's ongoing efforts in AI model development involve semi-automated processes rather than fully autonomous systems.

Watch for any further announcements from Google or its competitors regarding advancements in AI RSI. Developments in Google's DeepMind programs, particularly around the Gemini 4 Argon model, could influence market perceptions. Additionally, any new performance benchmarks or releases from Anthropic, Meta, or other key players may shift confidence levels in the race for the best AI model by the end of October 2026.

data.title: Japan Joins the Data Center Rush. These Stocks Can Benefit. — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Craig Mellow

While the rest of the world frets about a data center hangover, financial and political, Japan is rushing to join the party. That could boost some stocks that have flown below radar.

A conservative Japan Inc. largely sat out the rush to cloud computing that powered Data Centers 1.0, preferring to keep information on their own servers, says Hisashi Arakawa, head of Japan equities at Aberdeen Investments. That's left the No. 4 economy way behind as 2.0 revs up. Japan's gross domestic product is one-seventh the size of the U.S. Its data center use is one-seventeenth in gigawatt terms, the International Data Center Authority reports.

Investors have plans to fill the gap. Just this month, U.S.-based artificial intelligence A-listers Anthropic and Dell unveiled multibillion-dollar Japanese data center projects, in partnership with NTT and local power generator Jera, respectively. Private-equity giant Blackstone laid out its own $30 billion Japanese agenda in June.

Part of the draw is an emphatic YIMBY attitude from Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's government, which flagged AI infrastructure as a priority for the $2.3 trillion, 15-year strategic investment plan it announced this summer. "The government support will be about de-bottlenecking approvals, particularly in power generation," says Noriaki Saito, head of investment strategy at Global X Japan.

What could go wrong? Investors are relaxed about a consensus-oriented Japanese public catching the anti-data center fever that is roiling industry plans from Texas to Australia. "Resistance will probably be limited compared to other countries," predicts Keiichi Matsumoto, director of the government-linked Japan U.S. Venture Ecosystem.

Takaichi has effectively linked keeping data at home with national security as global cyberattacks and AI "accidents" increase. Aberdeen's Arakawa notes. Despite its famous population density, Japan has large tracts of abandoned rural land for data center siting, adds Neil Newman, head of strategy at Tokyo-based Astris Advisory. "More than 90% of Japanese live in urban areas," he says. "Rural areas are so empty, there is no one there to complain."

Japan's more acute challenge in the data center race is power, Newman says. Lacking its own fossil fuel resources, the country was aiming for nuclear power to provide half its electricity before the Fukushima disaster of 2011, he notes. The proportion today is less than 10%, leading to a sort of soft rationing for households. "You can't sell electric vehicles here because there's not enough power to charge them up," Newman says.

Takaichi has plans for a nuclear resurgence in the 2030s. Arakawa is skeptical. "The nuclear restarts have been quite political with local governments getting involved," he says.

While Anthropic and Dell are both aiming for the Tokyo-Osaka metropolitan belt, the northern island of Hokkaido is emerging as a land of the data center future, combining wide open spaces, wind power, and temperatures that minimize cooling costs. SoftBank Group and Toyota Group subsidiary Eurus Energy are among the heavy hitters moving forward there.

Arakawa sees Japanese data center capacity doubling over the next few years, a relatively conservative estimate. That should lift the shares of overlooked electrical engineering contractors like Kraftia and Kandenko, he predicts. "We are seeing double-digit order growth and rapid market expansion in this subsector," he says.

Other Japanese names already play unheralded but critical roles in the global data center supply chain and stand to benefit from domestic expansion. Global X's Saito flags Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, a top producer of turbines for natural gas-powered electricity generators, and Daihen, which makes transformers for power grids. Arakawa adds Daihen competitor Fuji Electric and Sumitomo Electric Industries, a standout manufacturer of the optical cables that thread through data centers.

"As long as the supply chain is paid, all these companies will be fine," Neil Newman comments.

One indication of how fast and far Japan will move on data centers should come by year's end, when a Takaichi budget attaches some concrete yen amounts to her strategic investment priorities, which number no less than 17.

Standing still doesn't seem like an option, though, for a Japan increasingly convinced it needs to stand on its own. "The geopolitical backdrop matters more than a decade or two ago," Saito says. "Having data centers within Japan seems more important nowadays."

data.title: How Trump's energy dominance turned into hubris: Bousso
data.description:
By Ron Bousso

When Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025, “energy dominance” was the bedrock of his economic and foreign policy plans. But an unpopular war with Iran and soaring household fuel costs have now made energy policy a major liability for the US president heading into next month’s midterm elections.

Ironically, it was the US position as the world's top oil and gas producer, perhaps more than anything else, that enabled Trump to pursue foreign policy goals that may turn out to be the costliest of his political career.

In the first two years of Trump’s second term, vast US oil and gas resources emboldened Washington abroad, strengthened its hand in trade disputes and underpinned a broader effort to restore US geopolitical dominance.

Yet the Iran war exposed the central weakness in that vision: dominating energy production does not mean controlling energy prices.

What began as a pursuit of US energy independence evolved into a doctrine of energy dominance. That is now looking like energy hubris.

UNLEASHING AMERICAN ENERGY

The foundations of Trump’s strategy were laid long before his return to office last year. The development of cost-effective techniques to tap the country's onshore shale basins transformed the US into the world’s largest producer of natural gas in 2009 and petroleum in 2018. By 2022, it was the leading exporter of liquefied natural gas, giving Washington unprecedented influence over global energy markets.

US crude production rose from around 5.5 million barrels per day in 2010 to nearly 14 million bpd today, around a fifth of global supplies, while the country also accounts for more than a quarter of global LNG exports. No single nation has ever occupied such a commanding position in the global energy system.

Trump sought to turn that advantage into a governing doctrine.

On his first day back in office, he declared a national energy emergency and ordered the government to “unleash American energy”, prioritising oil, gas, coal and nuclear power while sidelining renewables.

Within weeks, he made “energy dominance” official US policy, establishing the National Energy Dominance Council and reviving his familiar “drill, baby, drill” slogan as the purported cure for elevated inflation and economic anxiety. In an October 2025 proclamation, Trump summed up the philosophy as “maximum production, maximum prosperity, and maximum power”.

ENERGY POLICY IS FOREIGN POLICY

This doctrine extended far beyond domestic energy policy.

The administration’s national security strategy, published last December, explicitly linked US influence in the Western Hemisphere to energy dominance, drawing on the 19th-century Monroe Doctrine that sought to oppose European political intervention in the region.

In a little over a year, the administration wielded US oil and LNG exports in trade negotiations, promoted energy deals as part of efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war, and highlighted Greenland’s resource wealth in a push for greater influence over the Arctic territory.

The high-water mark for Trump’s energy doctrine arguably came early this year after Washington removed Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in a swift military operation.

The US subsequently took control of Venezuelan oil exports and revenues, forced through changes to the country’s hydrocarbons legislation that displaced Chinese companies, and secured an unprecedented agreement granting it access to a fifth of Venezuela’s oil reserves.

By February, Trump’s vision of building an economy and foreign policy around abundant fossil fuel resources appeared to be taking root. The US possessed not only more energy than any rival, but also the ability to use that abundance to shape trade, diplomacy and security.

Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran in late February put that doctrine to the test.

THE IRAN QUAGMIRE

The president initially claimed that the joint campaign with Israel against Iran would last only a few weeks. He also repeatedly indicated that vast US oil and gas resources, together with newfound access to Venezuela’s oil wealth, would shield the economy from any resulting spike in energy costs, which he also suggested would be brief.

Those assumptions have not aged well.

The war launched on February 28 led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly one-fifth of global energy supplies used to flow, triggering one of the largest energy disruptions in modern history. Middle Eastern producers cut output and rerouted exports where possible, while major importers across Asia reduced consumption.

This caused oil prices to nearly double in the first two months of the conflict, with global benchmark Brent crude peaking at $118 a barrel in March.

That was well below the record $145 reached in 2008, when Iran-related geopolitical tensions, surging Chinese demand and a weakening US dollar drove prices higher. It was also far less than many had feared, largely thanks to reduced Chinese oil imports, ample crude stocks and the surprising adaptability of global markets. But it still represented a severe shock.

Moreover, the risk premium from the Iran war is becoming entrenched. Even though crude flows from the Middle East have mostly recovered, Brent is trading around $110.

The conflict has also spread across the Middle East, pulling in most of Washington's Gulf allies, most notably the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia, which have suffered multiple deadly attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis. This has upended the market’s confidence in the security of Middle Eastern crude, unravelled longstanding supply routes and sent shipping prices skyrocketing.

Trump wanted to put his stamp on global energy markets, but this was clearly not what he had in mind.

PAIN AT THE PUMP

In one respect, the 2026 energy shock has vindicated Trump’s strategy. The war cemented the US position as the world’s top supplier of crude, refined fuels and LNG, delivering enormous profits to domestic producers and exporters and allowing the US to expand its position in the global market.

Energy independence certainly offered US consumers some protection against the energy shock, particularly compared with Asian economies, where prices and demand destruction were much more extreme this year.

But that protection has been far from ironclad.

US gasoline prices at the pump climbed above $4.60 a gallon in May, the highest level since 2022, while diesel surged to a record $6.50 a gallon in September as global refining capacity was squeezed.

Those increases rapidly became a political problem for the White House as cost-of-living concerns moved to the forefront of the campaign ahead of the midterms on November 3.

The administration sought to contain the fuel-price spike by pulling almost every available lever, including easing biofuel blending mandates and, most controversially, reaching a diesel supply agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

This dynamic underscores the difference between commanding supply and controlling prices.

Oil, LNG and refined fuels are internationally traded commodities. US producers sell them at prices shaped by global supply and demand. They don’t typically reserve cheap energy for American households.

While Trump briefly floated the idea of a diesel export ban, officials ultimately rejected it. Even though a ban might have brought down domestic prices initially, it would likely have resulted in higher fuel prices over the medium term due to global market dynamics.

‘ENERGY SECURITY IS NATIONAL SECURITY’

The administration’s assertion last October that “energy security is national security” appears more relevant than ever. The Iran war has shown that cheap and reliable energy is essential for economic growth, whether it powers heavy industry or the data centres underpinning the artificial intelligence race.

But the conflict has also changed the meaning of energy security.

For countries dependent on imports, particularly many in Asia, the shock has revealed the risks of relying heavily on distant suppliers, vulnerable shipping routes and a concentrated global refining system. Their response is likely to be broader diversification: securing more suppliers, expanding domestic fossil fuel production where possible, accelerating renewable power and shifting more transport towards electricity.

That will not kick the US off its lofty energy perch, but it will likely weaken the allure of oil and gas for many countries over the coming years.

Trump likely felt emboldened to embark on the Iran war — something his predecessors had baulked at — precisely because US energy independence made a Middle East adventure seem less risky than it had when the US was heavily reliant on Gulf oil and gas.

But the conflict has, perhaps permanently, undermined Trump’s promise that energy dominance would guarantee low prices and economic security at home.

Hubris can be a dangerous thing.

data.title: France's luxury stores board up windows ahead of fresh protests
data.description:
Key points:
  • Rolex, De Beers among Parisian stores closed on day of protests
  • Luxury stores add security staffing, board up windows
  • Industry already grappling with slowing demand

By Alessandro Parodi

Luxury boutiques in France boarded up their normally glitzy windows and added guards ahead of fresh protests on Saturday, with some planning to stay closed after rioters looted shops across the country last weekend.

France, the most visited country in the world, draws large numbers of overseas shoppers seeking Chanel handbags and Hermes scarves, an important source of revenue for brands facing slowing demand.

But some decided staying open was too risky after last week's events, when rioters smashed and looted hundreds of shops in Paris, Marseille and Bordeaux.

A Rolex retailer and a De Beers store near the capital's famous Place Vendome will remain closed on Saturday, staff said, while managers at stores including Richemont-owned IWC said they would decide whether to close early depending on the intensity of the protests.

Groups including France's main student union UNEF and the Yellow Vest group, which emerged as a potent anti-establishment movement in 2018, plan to march through central Paris later on Saturday to protest against high living costs and cuts to public services.

NOT IN THE MOOD

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said on Friday that his ministry would deploy 70,000 police officers, backed by specialist units, to prevent the violence that occurred last week.

But staff at LVMH brands Louis Vuitton, Dior and Bulgari said they weren't taking any chances and security at their stores near Place Vendome had been increased for the day. Additional private security to supplement the police presence in the neighbourhood is also planned.

Nearby department store Printemps also increased its security staff, carried out safety repairs and added security measures to reinforce shop windows and entrances, a spokesperson for the store said.

Hermes finance chief Eric du Halgouet said this week the company had increased security measures at its French stores, adding it was too early to say how much impact recent events would have on business.

The image-conscious industry can ill afford further negative publicity. Consumer sentiment is gloomy worldwide and tourism is slowing as a result of the Iran war — contributing to disappointing quarterly reports at LVMH , Hermes and Kering this month.

Lidiya Shevchenko, a sales assistant at a Graziella Braccialini store, said she doubted many people would be looking to visit stores anyway during the protests.

"I suppose the mood is just as important when it comes to shopping," Shevchenko said.

One tourist who has already been put off is Cambodian Jerry Lay, who purchased several items from Louis Vuitton on the Champs-Élysées earlier this week.

"We do enjoy shopping in France, but after experiencing the protest (last Saturday), I'd say it's 50/50 whether I would consider coming back next time," Lay said.

data.title: ICRA retains eMudhra ratings, but flags regulatory and reputational risks after security breach
data.description:
Credit rating agency ICRA has retained its ratings for Bengaluru-based eMudhra Ltd after a security incident in its global website certificate business, but flagged potential reputational damage, regulatory uncertainty and risks to customer retention.

In an update dated October 23, ICRA retained its ratings at [ICRA]A (Stable)/[ICRA]A1 on the company's ₹35 crore unallocated credit limits.

The incident involved a flaw in the generation of security keys for eight intermediate authorities that verify website certificates. The issue led to browser makers blocking the affected authorities and eMudhra revoking the certificates. The company's board subsequently decided to exit the global certificate business and focus on its core enterprise solutions and other trust services.

The agency said the direct financial impact of eMudhra's decision to exit the global Secure Sockets Layer/Transport Layer Security (SSL/TLS) certificate business was likely to be limited, as it contributes about 1% of consolidated revenue.

However, ICRA cautioned that the impact could extend beyond the revenue from the business being discontinued. It said the incident could affect customer acquisition and retention in eMudhra's enterprise solutions business and overseas markets, which account for 64% of its revenue.

The agency also flagged uncertainty over the regulatory investigation and the possibility of past misuse of the weak keys, which could lead to third-party claims and further reputational damage.

ICRA said the company's net debt-free position and strong liquidity provide a cushion against the costs of exiting the business and any near-term disruption.

The company has stated that no data was breached and its Indian Digital Signature Certificate and eSign businesses remain unaffected. In an interview with CNBC-TV18 on October 22, Kaushik Srinivasan, Co-founder of eMudhra, called the cybersecurity lapse as a “one-off incident on a bad day”.

ICRA said it would continue to monitor the outcome of the regulatory review, eMudhra's business momentum and order inflows in the coming quarters.

data.title: Markets Espresso: Gabbar Singh Yeh Kehkar Gaya...Jo Darr Gaya, Wo Marr Gaya!
data.description:
Hello Espresso Lovers! We're back after what has been a very gruelling week. In cricket, we have something known as the "Commentator's Curse", where a Commentator praises a batsman or bowler and the batsman gets out the very next ball or the bowler bowls a very poor ball immediately after the praise. Human life is no different. Last Sunday, we were happy about the fact that this is supposed to be a truncated week. But the newsflow made a four-day week seem like eight, with no end in sight!

Possibly the most iconic character Hindi Cinema ever created was Gabbar Singh, Vald Hari Singh. He gave us so many memorable lines (from the fireball pen of Salim-Javed, of course), that they possibly fit into every instance in our life. As the Gen Zs would say, it is Gabbar Singh's world, and we just happen to live in it. We live in times where there is fear almost everywhere. The fear of a bear market, the fear of war, the fear of a recession, job losses - From "Zindagi ka Dusra naam Problem hai", we have transitioned to "Zindagi ka Dusra Naam Darr hai"!

Last week, we were optimistic, hopeful, relieved about a recovery taking place. That optimism and hope has been washed away in four days. The Nifty bled, but it was the broader markets that bled and some more. 99 out of 100 and 90 out of 100 - If these were our scores in Algebra and Geometry in our childhood, our parents would be really proud. But no. These are the number of stocks in the Nifty Midcap and Nifty Smallcap index respectively, which ended with losses on Friday. It was not just Friday, that's the story of the entire week. It is almost as if the bears dressed up as Gabbar Singh and demanded, "Yeh recovery, humko de de Bulls. Yeh Recovery Humko de de!"

The market may be battered and bruised, but there is one thing we have to admit. The market has depth. IPOs like Jio Platforms are proof of that. A ₹30,000 crore issue, in a weak market, where there is selling in almost every sector, ends up getting bids worth nearly ₹5 lakh crore (Ex-Anchor Book). That's putting money where the mouth is for you. Jio Platforms also went on to achieve many more records during the three-day bidding period, and next week will be even more important for the company, as the allotment takes place for eligible shareholders on Monday and the mega listing happens on Wednesday, October 28.

At the end of the day, there will be higher and lower oil prices, higher and lower bond yields, higher and lower interest rates, but what ultimately moves the market is EARNINGS. Just as KARMA is a five-letter word, EARNINGS is exactly the same word, but in seven letters. Gabbar Singh's entry sequence in Sholay shows him putting a gun to the head of his three men, and the gun doesn't fire on either of them. Put International Gemmological Institute, Tata Tele and L&T Tech instead of the three men. Good earnings, Teeno bach gaye! Reported weekly gains at a time when almost everything on the screen was red. Now replace them with Swiggy, Himadri Specialty Chemicals and KEI Industries. The street doesn't like the numbers, the gun fires on all three of them, and the result? All of them down between 20% and 25% for the week. Sazaa mili, baraabar mili.

Then comes the next fear. AI. But right now, it's not AI that is causing the fear, the theme itself is worried, scared, tense. The trade has begun to unwind. Why? Too many things to be about any one in particular. Some disappointing results, the excessive debt taken up by some companies and the yields on that debt reaching levels of distress, companies announcing more spending plans when even the current ones have not reached fruition yet, and if all of that was not enough, there is cybersecurity. Who bore the brunt of this? The retail guys. They always do. JPMorgan says retail loaded up on these semiconductor and memory chip makers last week, and they got smashed in this one. But what will retail do? They'll buy more at the earliest opportunity. They always do. Their hope and optimism sometimes put even those words to shame.

Since we were on Cybersecurity, the casualty of the week has been eMudhra. Private keys associated with its certificates were compromised. It's too technical a subject to explain in non-technical language. So we left this task to our friend Ashmit Kumar, who does it beautifully in this video. The management, though, called it a "one-off incident on a bad day." The market definitely did not think of it that way. Two straight days of 20% lower circuits and an exit from the business that the issue was associated with - the reactions to a "one-off incident on a bad day" are never so extreme. Hear out the management also speak to us on this issue and the defence they put up in this video.

Just as we have FOMO and JOMO, there should be a FODT too. The Fear Of Donald Trump. We just don't know when he wakes up and writes something on Truth Social that sends everybody around helter-skelter, announces something that nobody has a clue about, or says something outlandish in a rally that leaves people scratching their heads. Tariffs, a war that will now enter month No. 9, an election to face, and the lowest approval rating on record, the man has turned the world on its head in 2026 but remains hopeful of a Nobel Peace Prize. Think about it, jab 50-50 kos door koi ultra-bullish ya bearish ho jaata hai, to log kehte hai, bete Truth Social dekh le, Trump kuch likh dega!

We get into the business end of the earnings season next week. Multiple Nifty results, broader market names, the Fed rate decision, monthly expiries, and so much more. And then there is the market volatility and geopolitical tensions to grapple with anyway. We'll be on top of things as always. You don't need to fear about that part for sure! Subscribe to our newsletter, follow us on our social media handles, and you'll get the latest brew, the fastest and the most accurate!

Investing is difficult. Especially for smaller investors. The constant fear, especially in scenarios like these - whether the market will recover? Should I put money in now? Should I go all in or do it in a staggered way? What if the market falls more after I invest? What if the stocks I invest in fall more? But such is the market, right? And Such is life too. And who better than Gabbar Singh, Vald Hari Singh to tell us the biggest principle to overcome any fear we have, whether it be in life or for the markets - Jo Darr Gaya, Samjho Marr Gaya!

data.title: Windward Bio Group Files For U.S. IPO
data.description:
WASHINGTON (dpa-AFX) - Windward Bio Group AG, a clinical-stage biotechnology company focused on developing ultra-long-acting antibody medicines for serious respiratory and dermatologic diseases, has filed for an initial public offering in the United States.

In a regulatory filing, the Basel, Switzerland-based company disclosed plans to list its common shares on the Nasdaq Global Market under the ticker symbol 'WWB.' However, Windward Bio has not yet revealed the number of shares it plans to offer or the expected price range for the IPO.

Since its founding in 2024, Windward Bio has raised up to $365 million through equity financings backed by several leading global healthcare investors, including OrbiMed, Novo Holdings, SR One, Omega Funds, Blue Owl Healthcare Opportunities and RTW Investments.

Windward Bio is developing a portfolio of ultra-long-acting antibody therapies targeting conditions such as asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and atopic dermatitis. The company operates from its headquarters in Basel, Switzerland, and maintains operations in the United States.

data.title: Apple’s iPhone Duo hits stores in face of short supply and high demand
data.description:
Apple Inc. quickly sold out of its limited in-store inventory for the new iPhone Duo, underscoring the strong demand for a foldable device that starts at nearly $2,000.

The phone went on sale Friday, bringing back the once-familiar sight of people lining up overnight to get their hands on it first. Marking the company’s most radical reinvention in the iPhone’s nearly two-decade history, the Duo is a major bet that Apple can establish itself in a category that’s remained a niche so far.

Apple’s latest gadget packed stores from New York to Beijing and Singapore. The early turnout featured customers collecting their preorders, some trying their luck to secure limited inventory for walk-in purchases, and resellers hoping to flip the devices for a higher price.

In Singapore, a few hundred people stood in line early Friday, including a family of seven from Myanmar who’d camped out overnight.

“This is the first true innovation Apple have had in years,” said Peter Ingram, a chief technology officer visiting from London, who plans to buy it upon his return to the UK. “It is expensive. But I tried it out, played with it in the store. It’s incredible how it’s got no crease.”

In the US, Apple stores received roughly 50 to 200-plus Duo units per location, and they went fast. A store in Los Angeles had no units left for people who arrived after around 6:30 a.m. The 256-gigabyte star white model, priced at $1,999, was popular with shoppers.

Large crowds on launch day have mostly dissipated in recent years after Apple, retailers and wireless carriers began maintaining enough inventory to fulfill most orders through home delivery or appointment-based store pickups. But the company’s first foldable device arrived in much more limited supply.

Consumers placing new orders for the Duo on Apple’s website are now being offered delivery at the end of January, though some have seen their shipping estimates move up to as soon as November or December. The delays mark some of the lengthiest for a new Apple product in the company’s modern era.

Shoppers at the Domain Northside Apple Store in Austin were greeted by new Chief Executive Officer John Ternus, CBS reported. At the Fifth Avenue location in New York, the line was already stretching multiple blocks around 5 a.m., three hours before doors opened to iPhone Duo customers. The launch there was marked by Greg Joswiak, Apple’s senior vice president of marketing, and Vanessa Trigub, vice president of retail stores.

At the Apple Store in Lawrence Township, New Jersey, about 40 miles outside Philadelphia, the 256- and 512-gigabyte configurations sold out within the first half hour, leaving the pricier 1- and 2-terabyte models.

Victor Osorio, a shopper at that location, said even though foldables aren’t new, “Apple always does something different and adds extra spice to it. I’m not nervous about the form factor but I am about the hinge. I don’t want it to get in the way but it looks OK so far.” Osorio arrived early with his partner, Victoria, who also purchased the Duo and said she was intrigued by the device’s multitasking capabilities.

At the same location, Naveed Abubacker said he trades in his iPhone every year. “Foldable technology has been around for a while and Apple is late to the gate but I’m ready for it,” he said. “If it doesn’t work out for me, I’ll return it.”

In China, Shanghai and Beijing saw a moderate turnout, with most Duo buyers already loyal Apple customers who said they were excited to try out the new design. Many had to register in advance to secure their unit.

“It will take some getting used to,” said Andy Shen at Apple’s Sanlitun store in Beijing. “I chose the Duo mainly because it opens up to a bigger screen to enable better experience with videos, though its other functions are not measuring up to earlier generations, like the camera.”

As one of the most expensive mainstream smartphones ever sold, the Duo had raised questions about just how much demand there would be. Most of the shoppers in Beijing and Singapore looked past the high price and focused on the promise of a truly new Apple product after many years of iterative updates.

The iPhone lineup is Apple’s largest moneymaker, generating roughly half of the company’s revenue. And the Duo is the biggest single design change in the device’s nearly history. Though the company wasn’t first to market with a foldable phone, it looks to gain an edge with a more polished product built for Apple fans.

Rather than a repeat of the lackluster debut of the Vision Pro headset nearly three years ago, the Duo’s launch is shaping up to be a throwback to the iPhone introductions of old — when demand far outstripped supply. That’s the case even with device prices reaching as high as $3,199 for models with 2 terabytes of storage.

Though the Duo’s cost sets a record for a mass-market smartphone, Apple’s competitors such as Samsung Electronics Co., Xiaomi Corp. and Oppo have been raising prices as well. Shortages of memory chips and other components have made consumer electronics more expensive across the board.

The new phones from Apple are difficult to produce because of their advanced hinge and new display technology. They’re also only built in a limited number of facilities in China. Apple expanded production in recent years for its traditional iPhones, including to India, which has helped with supply.

Apple reports its quarterly earnings results on Nov. 2, but those won’t include sales of the Duo because the period concluded around the end of September. It will reflect early sales of iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max models, which debuted on Sept. 18.

Other new versions, such as the entry-level iPhone or the updated Air, won’t go on sale until next year, Bloomberg News has reported. That marks a change in the company’s usual release schedule, a move meant to help spread out revenue across the year.

data.title: 25 years of agricultural transformation: From Gujarat’s growth journey to farmer prosperity
data.description:
Over the past 25 years, Indian agriculture has undergone a foundational shift largely driven by investments in irrigation, rural infrastructure, farm technology and direct grower support. Under Narendra Modi’s leadership, first in Gujarat and later at the Centre, strengthening rural livelihoods has remained central to India’s development trajectory. This productive capacity is reflected in the nation’s food grain output, which reached an estimated record of 357.73 million tonne in 2024-25.

The next chapter of this journey requires a broader benchmark of success. While national food security remains fundamental, agricultural progress must also translate into sustainable farm incomes, healthier soils, disciplined water use and greater economic resilience for the smallholder.

Gujarat’s experience: Development through ground-level action

Gujarat’s agrarian turnaround offers valuable lessons on how water governance, rural infrastructure and community engagement can strengthen agricultural productivity in arid regions. Measures such as water conservation, combining the Sardar Sarovar canal work with decentralised check dams, farm ponds and micro-irrigation, helped alleviate chronic water scarcity across the State. Alongside water infrastructure, the Jyotigram Yojana and Krishi Mahotsav brought agricultural scientists directly to village doorsteps before the sowing season.

The grassroots principle of khet ka pani khet mein, gaon ka pani gaon mein (retaining field water in the field and village water in the village) captures a lasting truth: water security begins with local resource management.

Subsequent national programmes supporting micro-irrigation under PMKSY, direct income liquidity via PM-KISAN, and crop risk insurance have further expanded the scope of this agriculture across India. The priority now is ensuring that macro-level infrastructure consistently translates into better farm-gate decisions.

Beyond production: The farmer income imperative

Today, the central challenge facing Indian agriculture is no longer simply producing more; It is about ensuring that higher output generates remunerative and sustainable net returns.

Fragmented landholdings, rising cultivation costs, mandi price fluctuations and post-harvest loss continue to squeeze farm margins. Because sowing decisions often remain disconnected from market signals, bumper harvests frequently trigger farm-gate price crashes - even as India remains heavily dependent on imports for edible oils and pulses. Correcting this demand-supply mismatch requires placing market intelligence, crop diversification, warehousing and cold-chain infrastructure at the heart of agricultural planning.

Climate volatility adds another layer of urgency. Unseasonal downpours during harvest, terminal heat stress and shifting pest cycles mean that traditional calendar-based farming is no longer viable. Efficient irrigation, balanced soil nutrition, Integrated Pest Management (IPM) and real-time weather advisories are now operational necessities to protect farm profitability.

Science, trust and the last mile

Agricultural innovation delivers its full value only when it reaches farmers in an actionable and accessible form. In crop protection, our guiding principle is straightforward: spray right, not spray more. Accurate pest identification, choosing the right molecules, adhering to recommended doses and timely application are vital to cutting cultivation costs while protecting crops.

For the agri-input industry, responsibility extends far beyond supplying products. Building last-mile literacy through deeper partnerships with State agricultural universities, extension networks and Krishi Vigyan Kendras can turn laboratory research into daily field practice.

Equally critical is protecting the farmers from the menace of counterfeit and sub-standard agrochemicals, which destroy both crop yields and grower trust. Eliminating spurious inputs requires a coordinated push: stricter statutory enforcement, faster state laboratory testing of all the companies and not biased sample analysis of selected companies, farmer awareness drives and end-to-end digital authentication, which includes QR-code traceability – which is mandatory across the supply chain. Simultaneously, scaling precision technologies like agricultural drones that reduce water consumption by up to 80-90 per cent and minimise applicator exposure will accelerate field-level efficiency when backed by proper training.

Defining the next 25 years

India’s agricultural journey over the past quarter-century secured the nation’s food bowl security. The next 25 years must strengthen the economic prosperity of those who fill it with food.

Achieving that transition requires sustained alignment among policymakers, agricultural scientists, the input industry and cultivators focused on maximising sustainable net returns per acre while safeguarding every drop of water and every inch of topsoil. Ultimately, the agricultural transformation will be judged not just by how much India grows, but also by how reliably its farmers prosper.

The author is Chairman Emeritus, Dhanuka Agritech Ltd.

data.title: Maharashtra Targets Chemicals Hub Near Wadhavan Port As Policy Nears Final Stage
data.description:
The state is considering acquiring up to 5,000 acres near Wadhavan port for a dedicated chemicals park as India targets a USD 1 trillion sector by 2040

Maharashtra is in the final stage of formulating a dedicated chemicals sector policy and aims to announce it by the first week of November, Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis said on Thursday. The state is also exploring the acquisition of 2,500–5,000 acres near the upcoming Wadhavan port in Palghar district to develop a dedicated chemicals park.

Speaking at an industry event organised by the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI), Fadnavis said the proposed policy would support the sector’s long-term growth. The state government has consulted industry leaders over the past few months to understand their requirements, with inputs expected to be incorporated into the policy.Among those consulted were Reliance Industries Executive Director Nikhil Meswani and UPL Chairman Jai Shroff. Fadnavis expressed confidence that the policy would encourage investors to expand their commitments to Maharashtra’s chemicals industry.

Chemicals Sector In Maharashtra

Fadnavis said the need for a dedicated chemicals policy became apparent after the state introduced its industrial policy last year. Maharashtra currently has 3,600 entities operating in the chemicals sector, which accounts for 19 per cent of the sector’s gross value added (GVA) and 17 per cent of chemical exports. The industry employs around 300,000 people in the state, he said.

He also highlighted Maharashtra’s existing port infrastructure, including Jawaharlal Nehru Port Authority (JNPA), which he described as the country’s largest container port, as a factor supporting the state’s role in the chemicals industry.

Proposed Chemicals Park Near Wadhavan

The state plans to develop a dedicated chemicals ecosystem near the greenfield Wadhavan port, which Fadnavis said is expected to be ready in about three years. The proposed land acquisition would support the establishment of a Bhavya Rasayanik Park, in line with the Union government’s announcement of Bhavya Rasayan Parks.

The proposed park is intended to create an industrial hub close to the port, supporting connectivity and the development of the chemicals sector.

India Targets USD 1 Trillion Chemicals Sector

Union Minister for Chemicals and Fertilisers J P Nadda, who also addressed the event, said the chemicals sector is currently valued at USD 220 billion, with a target of reaching USD 1 trillion by 2040.Nadda identified improved connectivity, supportive policies and industry leadership as factors that could contribute to the sector’s growth. He also said the government would facilitate environmental clearances for upcoming projects as part of its efforts to support capacity expansion.

The minister urged industry players to increase their focus on research and development (R&D). He added that advanced chemicals and petrochemicals are included in a newly launched Rs 1 lakh crore fund aimed at promoting research and innovation.

data.title: India's Scotch probe of Diageo, Pernod undermining India-UK pact benefits, trade group says
data.description:
Key points:
  • Indian investigators want firms to pay 150% duty on bulk Scotch, not 75%
  • Trade group says the pact’s tariff cut could become unavailable
  • Investigators searched Pernod, Diageo offices this month
  • Trade group seeks Indian commerce minister’s urgent intervention

By Aditya Kalra

India's move to exclude bulk Scotch imports from a reduced 75% tariff goes against provisions agreed in an India-UK trade deal, a group representing liquor makers Diageo and Pernod Ricard wrote in a letter seen by Reuters.

Whisky tariffs were a sticking point during the years of protracted negotiations leading up to the deal's July 15 implementation, though India ultimately agreed to halve import taxes on certain Scotch imports from 150% to 75% immediately and to 40% over 10 years.

The British government said "iconic UK products" like whiskies would benefit from the pact. Indian investigators, however, have privately told companies the reduced rate does not apply to bulk Scotch concentrates, creating the first significant dispute over the free trade agreement since it took effect.

India's Directorate of Revenue Intelligence searched the offices of Pernod and Diageo and questioned executives this month as part of an investigation into whether they misclassified imported products to benefit from the reduced rate.

CLASSIFICATION ISSUE RISKS UNDERMINING PACT, GROUP SAYS

In a letter to India's commerce minister on Friday, the International Spirits and Wines Association of India wrote that the classification issue "risks undermining, in practice, an important market-access benefit negotiated and agreed between India and the United Kingdom".

"The preferential tariff treatment negotiated ... could effectively become unavailable for these imports," continued the letter, a copy of which was seen by Reuters.

ISWAI declined to comment on its letter, while India's commerce ministry did not immediately respond.

Pernod, which counts India as its biggest market by volume, declined to comment. Diageo did not respond to a request for comment. Both told Reuters earlier this week that they were cooperating with Indian authorities carrying out the investigation.

In the British government's first comment on the controversy, a spokesperson said: "We are working with the government of India to resolve this issue to ensure UK businesses can export under the tariffs agreed in the trade deal."

Import tariff disputes have long been a sore point for foreign investors in India, who have in the past faced demands for large amounts of back tax. Such disputes have embroiled the likes of Samsung and Volkswagen.

Pernod faces antitrust cases in India and a $314 million back-tax demand from Indian authorities, who accuse it of undervaluing some imports. The company denies wrongdoing.

BIG IMPLICATIONS FOR INDIA'S DRINKS SECTOR

ISWAI's letter underscores the shockwaves the investigation has sent through India's $65 billion alcohol market. Britain accounts for almost 75% of India's imported spirits, primarily driven by Scotch whisky, according to Crisil Ratings.

Indian government inspectors have told companies that they do not benefit from the reduced 75% tariff on bulk imports of Scotch concentrates, which must be declared under a customs classification that attracts a 150% duty, three people with direct knowledge of the matter told Reuters.

Pernod and Diageo import bulk concentrates, mixing them with other ingredients to produce hugely popular Indian brands like Royal Stag, Blenders Pride and McDowell’s.

The three people said companies including Diageo and Pernod believe concentrates imported from Britain should benefit from the new, lower tariff. ISWAI said in its letter that the India-UK agreement expressly provides preferential tariff treatment for whisky under the relevant tariff lines.

An urgent clarification could ensure market-access benefits negotiated by India and Britain are realised "while avoiding uncertainty and disruption for legitimate industry participants", the letter said.

On Saturday, the UK-based Scotch Whisky Association told Reuters in a statement that the import of bulk Scotch is key to whisky’s overall success in India and that upholding the core principles of the bilateral pact is vital.

The association, which counts Diageo and Pernod's Chivas Brothers as members, added the industry was "committed to working in partnership with the UK and Indian governments on the smooth implementation of the deal", so its benefits are unlocked.
